extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York; voters and readers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (late-18th-century public audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and argumentative standards for selecting institutional forms for impeachment trials, appointments, and the election/independence of the executive (as argued in The Federalist Papers). Focuses on what structural features best secure liberty, accountability, and good administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as court of impeachments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate is the proper body to sit as a court for impeachments rather than the Supreme Court; the Supreme Court would have been an improper substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given: impeachments cannot be tied down by strict rules suitable to ordinary courts; there will be no jury in impeachment trials to stand between judges and the party; vesting the power in the Senate avoids committing the grave discretionary power to a small number of judges; the Senate, with concurrence of two thirds required for conviction, provides strong security for innocence. The chief justice presiding is a prudent mean to obtain some benefits of judicial participation without incorporating the entire Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vesting the same persons as accusers and judges in multiple proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who dispose of a person's fame and civil rights in one proceeding should not be the same persons who later dispose of life and fortune in another; making the same persons judges in both cases would deprive accused persons of the double security intended by a double trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same body judged both the impeachment and subsequent prosecution, bias from the first decision would likely carry into the second; juries are sometimes swayed by judges who have predetermined guilt. This argues against combining trial functions that would expose defendants to cumulative prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not create a separate permanent court of impeachments (practicality and cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composing an impeachment court wholly distinct from other departments (permanent officers at the seat of government or officers called from the states) is undesirable due to expense and practical inconveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A separate permanent body would be costly and unnecessary; a body summoned from the states would cause delays, difficulty of collecting dispersed men, injury to the innocent from procrastination, opportunities for intrigue and corruption, and possible detriment to the State from prolonged inaction. These practical objections counsel against instituting a new permanent tribunal for impeachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial intermixture of departments is acceptable for special purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim of separation of powers is compatible with a partial intermixture of departments for special purposes, provided they remain distinct and unconnected in the main.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some mixing (e.g., legislature judging impeachments) can be proper and necessary as a check between branches. The important principle is preserving the departments' general distinctness while allowing special joint agencies to provide mutual defense against encroachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-thirds concurrence as a safeguard in impeachment convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring the concurrence of two thirds of the Senate for conviction provides as complete a security to innocence as can be desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A supermajority requirement is presented as a structural protection against partisan or unjust convictions, making it difficult for a factious majority to punish political opponents unjustly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate's role in appointments limits its capacity for favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate's power in appointments is to advise and consent (ratify or reject nominations), not to itself choose appointees, which reduces the risk that its appointment authority will lead to indulgent judgments toward those it helped create.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the President nominates and the Senate only ratifies, the Senate cannot be presumed to feel excessive bias toward the objects of appointment; they may even prefer others but lack the power to choose directly. This structure mitigates claims that the Senate would be unduly indulgent of appointees whom it helped bring into office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess appointments clause must be read contextually and limited to officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's power to 'fill up vacancies that may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session' applies to officers whose appointments are not otherwise provided for by the Constitution and which shall be established by law — not to senators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual interpretation: the clause is supplementary to the general appointment clause and relates to 'officers' described therein; the Constitution elsewhere (Art. I, §3 and §4) expressly assigns filling Senate vacancies to State executives. Reading clauses in connection avoids misreading the President's temporary appointment power as extending to the Senate itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: State executives fill casual vacancies in the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: If vacancies in the Senate happen during the recess of a State legislature, the Executive of that State may make temporary appointments until the next meeting of the legislature, which shall then fill such vacancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This express constitutional provision is cited as conclusive evidence that the power to make temporary Senate appointments belongs to State executives, not to the President; it is used to rebut claims that the President can fill Senate vacancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint agency of President and two-thirds of Senate secures fidelity in treaty-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Security against corruption and perfidy in treaty formation is sought in the joint agency of the Chief Magistrate and two thirds of the Senate, relying on the numbers and character of those who make treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It would be impractical and improper to contemplate impeaching two thirds of the Senate for consenting to an improper treaty; instead, fidelity is secured by selecting proper agents and making it difficult for them to combine in an interest opposite to the public good. If corruption of leading members can be proved, the body has incentive to sacrifice the guilty to divert public resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral College design: have electors chosen by the people to reflect popular sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of the people should operate in the choice of the President by committing the right of making it, in the first instance, to men chosen by the people for that special purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than leaving election to preexisting bodies (which could be tampered with), selecting temporary electors chosen by the people preserves popular input while avoiding direct tumult and influence on the ultimate choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors should be a small deliberative body capable of discerning executive qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate election should be made by men most capable of analyzing the qualities adapted to the station and acting under circumstances favorable to deliberation; a small number of persons selected from the general mass will be most likely to possess the information and discernment requisite to such investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, elector bodies are more likely to deliberate well and combine reasons and inducements; talents for low intrigue that might carry a single-State favorite to victory are less likely to secure the esteem of the whole Union required for the presidency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors should assemble and vote within their State to reduce tumult and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors chosen in each State are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, and this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments than if all convened in one place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dispersal reduces the risk of widespread tumult and makes large-scale corruption or cabal more difficult; corruption requires time and means and is harder to effect across many dispersed electors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors must be free from federal office-holding bias
rubrics_metrics.description: All those 'who from situation might be suspected of too great devotion to the President in office' are excluded from eligibility as electors — no senator, representative, or other person holding a place of trust or profit under the United States can be an elector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding federal office-holders from the electoral body mitigates the risk of undue bias toward the incumbent and preserves the independence of the electors acting to choose the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of the Vice-Presidency and preserving Senate's casting vote
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice-President is chosen in the same manner as the President; having an extraordinary person in that office (rather than electing a senator from within) preserves the Senate's constant representation because selecting a senator as VP would exchange a state's constant vote for a contingent one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two considerations justify electing a Vice-President by the same national process: to preserve the Senate's consistent representation and because the Vice-President may become substitute for the President, so the same mode of appointment is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive independence via re-election by a special body of representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable that the Executive be independent for his continuance in office on all but the people themselves; making re-election depend on a special body of representatives deputed by the society for that single purpose secures this independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If re-election depended on other ongoing bodies, the Executive might sacrifice duty to secure favor; dependence only on a special electoral body reduces inducements to compromise official duty for political survival.
